findings.title: A return-type name taken from the JSON procedure description reaches Class.forName with no allowlist, initializing an attacker-named class
findings.evidence: Source: the constructor that builds the object from a parsed JSON document, ProcedureDescription(Map<String, Object> pm) at line 48, whose first statement is JSONUtil.tryFill(this, pm) (line 49) - a reflective bean fill executed before anything in the document is validated. Transformation: the bean property javaReturnType is public and its setter carries a side effect - setJavaReturnType(String) assigns the field and immediately calls computeReturnTypeAsJavaClass() (lines 92-95). Sink: that method compares the string against nine primitive names and, for every other value, falls through to Class.forName(javaReturnType) at line 122. There is no allowlist, no package restriction, no asSubclass constraint and no use of the three-argument form with initialize=false. The intended origin of this value is visible in the sibling constructor, which derives it locally by reflection: this.javaReturnType = m.getReturnType().getName() (line 73). That the setters are driven reflectively while parsing is stated by the file itself, on the neighbouring property: '/** Private API - used via reflection during parsing/loading */ public void setReturn(String value)' (lines 82-83).
findings.impact: The party that authors the procedure description chooses a class name that the consumer's JVM loads. Class.forName(String) is the one-argument form, defined as Class.forName(name, true, callerLoader): it resolves and *initializes* the class, so the static initializer of any class on the consumer's classpath runs while the description is being parsed, before the application ever invokes a procedure. The attacker therefore gets (a) execution of whatever static-initializer side effects exist on that classpath - the standard precondition for turning unsafe reflection into code execution, (b) forced loading of classes the application never intended to touch, and (c) a remotely triggered IllegalStateException thrown from inside a setter (lines 124-126), aborting the parse. Boundary crossed: author of the JSON service description -> the JVM of the library's consumer.
findings.preconditions: The consumer builds a ProcedureDescription from a document it did not author - for a JSON-RPC client, the service description obtained from the remote endpoint, or any JSON the application feeds to this public constructor or to the public setter. Escalation from class initialization to code execution additionally requires a class with exploitable static-initializer side effects on the consumer's classpath; no such class was demonstrated here, and that classpath belongs to the consumer, not to the library.
findings.recommendation: Stop resolving arbitrary names. Resolve the return type against a closed allowlist of the types the service is allowed to declare, or defer resolution to the point of use and perform it with Class.forName(name, false, loader) followed by an explicit asSubclass or package check, so that parsing a document never initializes a class. Apply the control where the string becomes a Class, not only inside setJavaReturnType: the reflected-Method constructor writes the field directly (line 73) and bypasses the setter, so a fix installed only in the setter leaves the two population paths inconsistent - which is also why getReturnType() returns null today on that path, since _javaReturnTypeAsClass is only ever assigned from the setter. Treat the root cause as an insecure default in exported API: a public bean property whose assignment loads a class is exactly the defect local-app.md SS5 (LOC-10) describes as landing in the consumer's CVE rather than in the library's.
findings.inference: The single inferred link: JSONUtil.tryFill was not delivered and was not read, so that the document key 'javaReturnType' is the one routed to setJavaReturnType is taken from the Java bean-property naming convention plus the file's own javadoc that these setters are invoked 'via reflection during parsing/loading' (line 82), not from the filler's code. Everything after the setter was read directly (lines 92-127).

triage.reason: No control stands between the string and the sink inside the audited unit: computeReturnTypeAsJavaClass (lines 101-127) constrains nothing beyond the nine primitive names. Both entry points - the public constructor at line 48 and the public setter at line 92 - are exported API of a published library, so any validation a particular caller performs is validation another caller can skip, and FP-01 explicitly excludes a control a caller may forget.

Traced backwards, the value is never a literal, a constant or an allowlisted enum on this path: it arrives either in the caller-supplied Map (line 48) or through the public setter (line 92), and in both cases its origin lies outside the class. The only origin that is not externally supplied is the reflected-Method constructor at line 73, which does not reach the sink.

The sink at line 122 is Class.forName(String) - the one-argument overload, contractually equivalent to Class.forName(name, true, callerLoader), so it initializes the class it resolves and runs its static initializer. It is not the three-argument form with initialize=false, the result is not narrowed by asSubclass, and it is not a parse-only lookup. The sink is dangerous in exactly the form it is reached.

The code sits in the production source set (src/main/java/...), on a public constructor and a public setter, with no debug flag, test fixture or environment guard anywhere on the path. No built artifact was delivered, so this is read from source - which is why the answer is a negative rather than an exculpating HOLDS, since FP-04 would require the shipped artifact as evidence.

The crossing is nameable, as local-app.md SS0 requires: the author of the JSON procedure description on one side, the JVM of the library's consumer on the other. Two of that section's principals apply at once - 'a file the tool is pointed at' (the description document) and 'a consumer of the library' (the application that inherits this default). This is not a single principal acting on its own data.

findings.limits: Does not establish code execution: no gadget class with an exploitable static initializer was identified, and none could be from here, because the classpath belongs to the consumer. Does not establish who supplies the document at runtime - JsonRpcClient and the transport were not delivered. Does not establish what JSONUtil.tryFill does with keys it cannot match. Nothing was built, run or reproduced: the finding rests on reading the delivered source.

findings.title: The params member of the JSON document is cast and dereferenced unchecked, so a malformed description escapes the constructor as an unchecked exception
findings.evidence: Lines 51-58: the map member is cast with the warning silenced - @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") followed by List<Map<String, Object>> p = (List<Map<String, Object>>) pm.get("params") - and the result is dereferenced on the very next line, params = new ParameterDescription[p.size()]. Three shapes of document break it, all of them shapes the sender chooses: a document with no 'params' member makes pm.get return null and p.size() throw NullPointerException at line 53; a document whose 'params' is a string, a number or an object throws ClassCastException at line 52; a document whose 'params' is a list of non-objects throws ClassCastException at the loop's implicit checkcast, line 55. The sibling constructor cannot fail this way: it takes the array length from m.getParameterTypes() (lines 67-68). The class's own accessor already tolerates the absent case - arity() returns 0 when params is null (line 136) - so the contract admits a description the constructor refuses to survive.
findings.impact: A malformed or hostile procedure description becomes an unchecked exception thrown out of a public constructor during parsing, instead of a typed parse error the caller can handle. The gain over simply not answering is marginal - the caller ends up handling a RuntimeException on its parse path rather than a declared protocol failure - and no memory or state corruption follows. It also breaks interoperability with any legitimate peer that omits 'params' for a zero-argument procedure.
findings.preconditions: The consumer parses a description document it did not author, and does not wrap this constructor in a catch for RuntimeException.
findings.recommendation: Validate the document's shape before casting: require 'params' to be present and to be a List, check each element is a Map, and raise a declared parse exception that names the offending member. Where a missing 'params' is legitimate, initialize the array empty rather than throwing - arity() (line 136) already expects that state.
findings.inference: The same single gap as F-001: the caller that supplies the map was not delivered, so that this constructor is reached with a document from a party other than the application itself is read from the class's declared purpose ('Description of a single JSON-RPC procedure', line 26) and from its Map-based constructor, not observed in the caller.

triage.reason: No unskippable layer validates the document first: the constructor is the exported entry point and its first shape check is the cast itself. A caller that validates the JSON beforehand is a control the next caller can omit, which FP-01 excludes.
The shape of the map is chosen entirely by whoever authored the document; nothing in this class constrains it, and the value is not a constant or an allowlisted structure anywhere on the path.
Same crossing as F-001, named per local-app.md SS0: author of the description document -> the consumer's JVM. It is not the application failing on its own input.

This is not a redundant layer with an equivalent elsewhere: the constructor is the only place the document's shape is examined, and the exception escapes into consumer code. Severity is held at low rather than raised, because a party able to send this document can already deny the client its answer; what it gains is an unchecked exception on a path expecting a typed error, which is marginal but real.

findings.limits: Does not establish availability impact beyond the aborted parse: whether the exception terminates a connection or consumer thread depends on JsonRpcClient, which was not delivered. Not reproduced - nothing was built or executed - so the three failure shapes are read from the Java semantics of the cast and the dereference, not from a run.
